1.desc:
The questions you ask, the answers from both models and the vote you cast are all recorded. That is the whole point of the service: to produce freely available preference data.

Before publication, a model reviews the conversations to spot those holding personal or sensitive data. Those conversations are kept out of the public dataset, but they are held in a dataset reserved for research. So the text is not anonymised: a conversation is either published as it stands, or not published.

That filter is a safeguard, not a guarantee. compar:IA cannot guess what you type into the prompt: do not enter anything that could identify you or a third party, and do not paste contact details or confidential documents.
1.title: What happens to my conversations?

2.desc:
Preference data is used to improve models during future training.

By blindly comparing the responses of two models, compar:IA users express their preferences, indicating which responses are most relevant. This preference data can be used to improve model alignment—that is, to train them to generate responses that are more in line with user expectations and preferences.

This is an iterative process, where the model gradually learns to generate better responses based on feedback from humans on the quality of the responses. By being exposed to preference data, models adjust their response style.
2.title: Does preference data have an immediate effect on model performance?

3.desc: The uniqueness of the data collected on the compar:IA platform is that it is in lower ressourced languages and corresponds to real-life user tasks. This data reflects human preferences in specific linguistic and cultural contexts. This data allows us to adjust the models to make them more relevant, accurate, and adapted to user needs, while attempting to address any biases or gaps.
3.title: Why are the votes on compar:IA useful?

4.desc: compar:IA positions itself as a low-ressourced language assessment and alignment tool for language models, focused on response quality and preference data collection, thus distinguishing itself from the global ranking approach of chatbot arena developed by lmsys.org and the ethical alignment of AI models of Prism Alignment Project .
4.title: What makes compar:IA different from other similar initiatives?

1.title: How are environmental metrics calculated?
1.desc:
compar:IA uses the EcoLogits (GenAI Impact) methodology, which applies life cycle assessment (LCA) principles under the ISO 14044 standard. It currently covers two items: inference, that is using the model to answer, and the manufacture of the graphics cards (raw material extraction, production, transport).

The energy calculation starts from the model's active parameters and the number of tokens produced. A regression, fitted on the public measurements of the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard, gives the energy the graphics card spends per token. The share of the server hosting the model is added, and the total is multiplied by the data centre's PUE, which accounts for cooling and losses.

The reference hardware is that of data centres: an 80 GB NVIDIA H100 card, an 8-card server drawing 1.2 kW, a three-year lifespan and batches of 64 requests handled in parallel. The number of cards depends on the memory the model needs.

The CO₂ equivalent then follows from that electricity use, multiplied by the emission factor of the electricity mix of the country where the model runs.

For proprietary models, whose size is not published, EcoLogits works from a range: the figures shown are estimates, and are flagged as such.

It is worth noting that methods for assessing the environmental impact of AI are still being built.

2.title: What does a model's energy class mean?
2.desc:
Every model gets a class from A to F, on the same principle as the energy labels on household appliances. It rests on a single figure: the energy needed to produce one million tokens.

  • A: under 100 Wh
  • B: 100 to 300 Wh
  • C: 300 to 1,000 Wh
  • D: 1,000 to 3,000 Wh
  • E: 3,000 to 10,000 Wh
  • F: over 10,000 Wh

The class depends mostly on the size of the model and on its architecture. A dense model uses all of its parameters for every answer. A mixture of experts model activates only part of them, so at equal total size it consumes less.

The class is there to help you choose. For many everyday tasks, a model rated A or B answers just as well as one rated E, for a fraction of the energy.

3.title: How many graphics cards does it take to run a model?
3.desc:
For each model, compar:IA shows the hardware it would take to run it: a smartphone, a laptop, a workstation with one graphics card, or a server with several cards.

The estimate starts from the memory the model needs to load its parameters, then divides it by 80 GB, the memory of an NVIDIA H100 card, the data centre reference. A model that needs 320 GB therefore fits on four cards.

This is an order of magnitude, not a production setup: the calculation counts neither the memory taken by the context nor the copies of the model deployed to absorb traffic. Above all it gives a concrete sense of what "large model" means, and of what remains usable on an ordinary machine.

4.title: Do environmental metrics take into account the energy mix of different countries?
4.desc:
Data center locations play a very significant role in AI's carbon footprint. If a model is trained or used in a country heavily dependent on fossil fuels, its environmental impact will be greater than if it is hosted in a country that uses mostly renewable energy.

The AI environmental impact analysis method developed by Ecologits (from GenAI Impact) incorporates data on the energy mix of the different countries where the servers are located. This allows for a more accurate and nuanced estimate of the actual carbon footprint of inference on different generative AI models.

5.title: Do environmental impact estimations take into account the resources used to train the models?
5.desc:
Many environmental impact metrics focus primarily on the impact of inference , that is, the use of AI models to answer queries. This approach may give the illusion that inference is less energy-intensive than model training. However, the reality is more complex. Consider the car analogy:

  • Building a car (training) is a one-time, resource-intensive process.
  • Each car journey (inference) uses less energy, but these journeys are repeated daily, and their number is potentially immense.

Similarly the cumulative impact of inference, across millions of users querying daily, is often signficantly greater than the impact of initial training This is why it is crucial that AI carbon footprint assessment tools consider the entire lifecycle models, from training to inference

1.desc: Yes, the internationalization of compar:AI is underway. We are starting with an expansion to three pilot countries: Lithuania, Sweden, and Denmark. This first phase will allow us to test the approach and adapt the interface to different European linguistic and cultural contexts. Eventually, the circle may expand to more European languages based on feedback from these pilot countries. The objective is to gradually build a true European digital common for human evaluation of conversational AI, with collaborative governance that remains to be defined between the different participating countries.
1.title: compar:IA initially focused on French: are there plans for other European languages?

2.desc: The development of a European platform for comparing conversational AI models offers several concrete advantages. It allows for the collection of preference data reflecting the real needs of European users, thus improving the relevance of model answers for this userbase. The publication of the datasets guarantees better representation of European languages and cultures, often underrepresented in global datasets and evaluations dominated by English. It also ensures compliance with European regulations (GDPR, AI Act) and integrates evaluation criteria aligned with European priorities such as environmental impact reduction and algorithmic transparency. Finally, it fosters the emergence of a competitive and autonomous European AI ecosystem.
2.title: What are the advantages of a specifically European preference collection platform?

1.desc:
The ranking rests on user votes and on nothing else. In each duel, two models answer blind and you pick the one you prefer.

Those duels feed a Bradley-Terry statistical model, which gives each model the level that best explains all the duels observed, expressed as an Elo score as in chess. Every score comes with a confidence interval: a model that has fought few duels holds a far less certain rank than one judged thousands of times.

By default the ranking is shown with style control, which cancels out the effect of presentation habits, answer length or formatting, so that only substance is compared. You can turn that control off and see the raw ranking.

It measures human preference on real uses, in European languages. It is not a knowledge test: a model leading here may be beaten on a technical exam.
1.title: How is the compar:IA ranking calculated?

2.desc: We choose models based on their popularity, diversity, and relevance to users. We pay particular attention to making open weights and different size models available.
2.title: How do you choose the models present in the arena ?

3.desc: Inference, meaning the ability to query the models, is payed for by the project. For most models, we use the Open Router and Hugging Face Inference Providers on a per-token usage basis.
3.title: How do you manage to keep this service free?

4.desc:
Quantized models are optimized to consume fewer resources by simplifying certain calculations while aiming for the best response quality.

Quantization is an optimization technique that involves reducing the precision of the numbers used to represent the parameters of an AI model. This allows to reduce the size of the model and to speed up calculations , which is particularly advantageous for inference on resource-constrained machines.
4.title: What are “quantized models” ?

5.desc:
A model's ability to speak multiple languages is related to the linguistic diversity of its training data, not to the country it was developed in . LLMs use huge corpora of data with many languages , but the distribution of languages in the training data is not uniform. An overrepresentation of English can lead to limitations in other languages. These limitations are visible, for example, in anglicisms or the inability to generate content in certain languages classified as "endangered" by UNESCO .

The accuracy and richness of a model's vocabulary depend on the data used for its training .
5.title: Is there a link between the nationality of the company or lab that created the model and its ability to speak several languages?

6.desc: Few stakeholders are “transparent” about the data sources used in training corpora. This information is often confidential for legal and commercial reasons.
6.title: Can we see the training data of the models?

1.desc:
Yes, if you turn on web search before sending your question in the arena. Both models then receive the same extracts from pages found online, along with their addresses, and answer from them. The sources used appear under your message.

Without web search, models answer only from what they learned during training: they check nothing online, so recent or very specific facts may be missing.

Web search adds text to the request sent to the models. It therefore raises the number of tokens processed, and with it the energy shown in the summary.
1.title: Can models search the web?

2.desc:
Not blindly. A language model produces the most plausible text, not the most accurate. It can state something false with the same confidence as something true, and invent a date, a quotation or a reference. This is called a hallucination, and no model is free of it.

Web search cuts the risk without removing it. The model then works from real pages, but it can misread them, draw a conclusion they do not support, or land on a source that is itself wrong. The sources are shown precisely so that you can check.

This is also what the comparator makes visible: when two models answer the same question and contradict each other, at least one of them is wrong. That disagreement is a useful reminder that a confident answer is not a checked answer.
2.title: Can I trust the answers?

3.desc:
With web search turned on, yes. The models then receive extracts from pages along with their addresses, and can point back to them. The sources used also appear under your message, so you can check them yourself.

Without web search, no. A language model on its own cannot cite the sources behind its answer. It predicts the most likely next word from the statistical distribution of its training data. It can pull together information from thousands of texts, but it keeps no record of where any of it came from. If it does hand you a reference, that reference may be invented.

This is the principle behind Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), of which compar:IA's web search is one form: give the model outside documents at answer time, so it can lean on them and cite them.
3.title: Can models cite their sources?

4.desc:
Have you asked the question: “Explain to me the latest trendy cheesecake recipe and cite your sources” and been disappointed with the answers? That's normal...

“Raw” conversational AI models cannot answer questions about the most recent news. They are trained on static datasets and cannot interact with the web or open links. They do not have the ability to update themselves in real time with events unfolding in the world. The information the model has access to is limited to the date of its last training.

Therefore, if you ask a question about a recent news event, the model will rely on outdated information, risking generating inaccurate answers.

In the case of Perplexity, Copilot, or ChatGPT, the so-called “raw” conversational AI models are combined with other system blocks that allow them to connect to the internet to access information in real time. These are called “conversational agents.”

On compar:IA, turn on web search before sending your question: the models then receive extracts from recent pages and can answer about current events. Without it, they stay limited to their training data.
4.title: If I ask a question about the latest news, can the model answer?

5.desc:
If you include a URL in a query, the conversational model will not be able to access it directly. Language models process the query text but do not have the ability to interact with the web or open links. They are trained on a fixed text dataset, and their answers are based on this training data. When a question is asked, the models use this training to generate an answer but cannot access new information online if they are not enabled to do so by a surrounding system.

As an analogy, imagine a student taking an exam without internet access. They can use their acquired knowledge to answer questions, but cannot visit websites for additional information.

Web search changes this in part: once turned on, it feeds the models the content of pages found online. It still does not open the exact address you paste, it runs a search from your message.
5.title: If I include an URL in a query, can the model access it?

6.desc: Raw conversational AI models answer directly by predicting tokens (words) based on their probability, while a search engine offers links and resources for the user to explore on their own.
6.title: What's the difference between asking a question to a conversation AI model and searching on Google?

7.desc:
The chatbot arena was designed and developed as part of a government startup led by the French Ministry of Culture, integrated into the Beta.gouv.fr program by the Interministerial Digital Directorate (DINUM). This initiative supports French public administrations in building useful, simple, and user-friendly digital services.

It is now funded by the Ministry of Culture, DINUM and the Alliance for Language Technologies (ALT-EDIC).

alignment.a: Alignment comes after a language model’s pre-training phase, acting as a final "refinement" or "polishing" step. During pre-training, the model learns to predict the next word, gaining the ability to generate coherent text - but alignment is what tailors it to human preferences.
alignment.b: The alignment phase trains the model to better meet human needs by making it more relevant (answering questions more accurately), more honest (admitting when it lacks sufficient data), and safer (avoiding harmful or inappropriate content).
alignment.c: Without alignment, an LLM might be technically capable yet impractical to use - failing to grasp what users truly expect in a conversation.
alignment.title: Alignment: a critical post-training phase

datasets.a: Alignment relies on highly specialized datasets, meticulously designed to teach the model "proper" behavior.
datasets.b: Preference data is a critical component of alignment, working alongside demonstration data (expert-crafted human-AI dialogues with precise tone/style guidelines), safety data (curated examples teaching models to reject harmful requests), and domain-specific datasets (tailored for fields like medicine, law, or education).
datasets.c: Preference data presents multiple potential answers to the same question, ranked by human evaluators based on criteria like relevance, usefulness, or harm potential. Users indicate which response performs best, and these curated datasets are then used to fine-tune models - aligning them with expressed human preferences.
datasets.title: Specific datasets

alignment.desc: Alignment: A bias-mitigation technique based on crowdsourcing user preferences to refine model behavior

diversity.a: To reflect the diversity of cultures and languages in model outputs, alignment datasets must incorporate a broad range of languages, contexts, and real-world user tasks. Diversifying alignment data ultimately improves a model’s performance in two key ways:
diversity.b: First, it reduces cultural bias by preventing a single - often Anglophone -perspective from dominating the AI’s responses. The model learns that valid answers vary by cultural context, recognizing multiple legitimate ways to address the same question.
diversity.c: Second, exposure to linguistic and cultural diversity enables context-aware responses: a French user gets advice tailored to France’s systems, while a Danish user receives information aligned with their national context.
diversity.d: The result? A more inclusive conversational AI - one that acknowledges and adapts to diverse cultural perspectives.
diversity.title: Diversify data sources to reduce bias

english.a: Preference data is expensive to produce because each example requires skilled human evaluation. Platforms like chat.lmsys.org help crowdsource these datasets—but few users contribute in their native language, leaving low-resource languages underrepresented.
english.b: Preference datasets for European languages are scarce - or nonexistent. In LMSYS’s dataset, for instance, French queries represent less than 1% of the total.
english.c: compar:IA is a chatbot arena designed to gather multilingual conversations - capturing region-specific cultural references like daily tasks, local culinary traditions, education systems, or historical and literary touchstones.
english.title: European languages suffer from a shortage of preference data

alignment.title: How can we reduce cultural and linguistic biases in these models?

diversity.desc: These biases can lead to incomplete or outright incorrect responses, sidelining the diversity of European languages and cultures.
diversity.title: Overlooked cultural and linguistic diversity

english.desc: Conversational AI relies on large language models (LLMs) trained primarily on English data, creating linguistic and cultural biases in their outputs.
english.title: Training data overwhelmingly in English

size.title: How many people can join an AI Duel session?
size.desc: We have run sessions with only 5 participants, and others in front of 300 people. The bigger the group, of course, the less each person gets to speak. That said, the workshop is very flexible: it comes down to how well the facilitator handles the room. A small group makes for a more personal experience; a large one brings real energy.

expertise.title: Do I need to be an expert to facilitate an AI Duel?
expertise.desc: Not at all. The facilitator guide is built so that anyone interested can run a duel. It covers the subject, what is at stake, and the tools you need to run the session. Having played with language models helps, but it is in no way required.

duration.title: How long does a Duel session last?
duration.desc: The shortest sessions we have run lasted 20 to 30 minutes, which does cut into the discussion. Ideally a good duel takes about 45 minutes. With 1h30 it is better still: you can run several duels and go deeper.

about.title: About the compar:IA day
about.event: The compar:IA day took place on 7 February 2025 at the BnF François-Mitterrand. Over 300 people attended in person and around a hundred more followed the live stream.
about.goal: The aim was to discuss the ethical, cultural and environmental stakes of conversational AI.
about.thanks: Many thanks to everyone who took part and to the partners of the event!
